extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate computer science or mathematics students (EECS 4315) learning how to write structured proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing clear, maintainable mathematical proofs by using explicit structure, naming, and by stating definitions and propositions clearly; aimed at students learning proof-writing conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure: sequence of named statements, each with a proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure: sequence of named statements, each with a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two principles to make proofs easier to understand: structure and naming. Present proofs as a sequence of clearly named statements (theorems, propositions, lemmas, etc.), and provide a proof for each named statement so the organization of the argument is explicit and navigable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming: sequential numbers
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign concise, sequential identifiers (numbers) to statements so they can be unambiguously referenced elsewhere in the text. This supports clarity and cross-referencing within a body of proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prose-only (17th-century) proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Today's “proofs are still written in prose pretty much the way they were in the 17th century.” ... These “proofs are hard to understand, and they encourage sloppiness that leads to errors.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on long-form narrative prose for proofs. Instead, use explicit structure and naming to reduce ambiguity and sloppiness; break arguments into named, checkable steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: State definitions explicitly before using them
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the formal definition of concepts you will use (example given: definition of an equivalence relation listing (reflexive), (symmetric), and (transitive)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always include the precise definition(s) relevant to the argument (with properties listed clearly) before attempting a proof that depends on them so that assumptions are explicit and readers can verify which axioms are in play.

rubrics_metrics.name: State propositions and tasks clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Label propositions and state tasks explicitly (example slides: 'Proposition: In the definition of an equivalence relation, reflexivity is redundant.' followed by 'Task: Prove the above proposition.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate the claim to be proved as a clearly labeled statement (Proposition/Theorem/Lemma) and, in pedagogical settings, state the task plainly so the goal of the proof is unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make explicit which assumptions/properties are used in a proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Example proof states 'Therefore, using only symmetry and transitivity, we obtain reflexivity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving a claim, explicitly indicate which assumptions, axioms, or properties you are using at each step (e.g., 'by symmetry' or 'by transitivity') so the logical dependence is clear and reviewers can check that no unstated assumptions are invoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow established best-practice references
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to Leslie Lamport's 'How to write a 21st century proof' is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt and cite modern, community-accepted guidance on proof presentation (e.g., Lamport's recommendations) to improve clarity and reduce common errors in proof writing.
